full_judgment:
Mr. Justice Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman, J: Rule was issued to show cause why the order of removal of the. writ petitioner from the office of Additional Judge of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh purportedly passed under Article 96(6) of the Constitution by the Hon'ble President of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh communicated vide Notification No. 996- Bichar-4/1 H-12/2003 dated 20.4.2004, evidenced by Annexure-H to the writ, petition being contrary to the findings of Supreme Judicial Council contained in its report on the enquiry conducted under. Article 96(4)(b) of the Constitution evidenced by Annexure-G to the writ petition, being required by the Honb’le President under Article 96(5)(b) of the Constitution. Evidenced by Annexure-F to the writ petition to the effect that the allegations against Mr. Justice Syed Shahidur Rahman are not proved beyond doubt ....... and there being no proof-of any allegation of "gross-misconduct" on the part of the writ petitioner shall not be declared to be without jurisdiction, lawful authority and of no legal effect; and why the opinion, as appearing in the enquiry report of the Supreme Judicial Council, to the effect that "Mr. Justice Syed Shahidur Rahman should not continue as an Additional Judge of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh" inspite of its finding of "non-proof" of the allegation brought against the writ petitioner, should not be declared to he beyond the scope of Article-96(5)(b) of the Constitution and hence is without jurisdiction and lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 4. In the writ petition it has been stated that being annoyed with the behaviour patterns of the President of the Supreme Court Bar Association in making allegation of receiving Tk. 50,000/- from a client to fix him a bail by a judge, the Hon'ble Chief Justice for Bangladesh required the said President of the Supreme Court Bar Association to let the Hon'ble Chief Justice know as to the precise nature of complaint against the judge concern by letter dated 6.10.2003, copy of which has been annexed as Annexure-C to the writ petition, and in reply thereto the President of the Supreme Court Bar Association by his letter dated 14.10.2003brought certain facts as to the conduct of the writ petitioner when he was the elected Treasure of the Bar Association and about the allegation of receiving Tk. 50,000/- as made by a Tadbirkar, named Mrs. Nasim Sultana Kona, copy of the reply has been annexed as Annexure-D to the writ petition. Thereafter on receipt of said reply dated 14.10.2003, the Hon'ble Chief Justice was pleased to inform the President of Republic about the allegations appearing in the newspapers and thereafter the Hon'ble President was pleased to direct the Supreme Judicial Council to enquiry into the allegations against the writ petitioner. The Supreme Judicial Council accordingly enquired into the allegation and submitted its report as required by the provisions of Article 96(4)(b) of the Constitution, copy of the report has been annexed as Annexure-G to the writ petition, and on receipt of the enquiry report, wherein the council held that "though the allegation against Mr. Justice Syed Shahidur Rahman are not proved beyond doubt but on consideration of the facts and circumstances and the materials on record in their entirety it cannot be said that there is total absence of material in support of the allegations nor can it be said that the allegations are without any basis. Therefore, in our opinion Mr. Justice Syed Shahidur Rahman should not continue as an Additional Judge of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh" the Hon'ble President was pleased to remove the petitioner from his office purportedly in exercise of his powers conferred by Article 96(6) of the Constitution and the said impugned order of removal was communicated to the writ petitioner by the notification No. 996-Bichar-4/1H-12/2003 dated 20.4.2004, which has been annexed as Annexure-H to the writ petition. On receipt of the said notification the writ petitioner made an endeavour to obtain certified or true copy of the proceedings, including the report, of the Supreme Judicial Council but without any success. However the petitioner obtained a copy of the inquiry report of the Supreme Judicial Council (Annexure-G) through a Newspaper correspondent, which was circulated through a web-site, and which fact was published in "The Daily Bhorer Kagoj" dated 7.3.04 and there being no rejoinder there against, the petitioner accepted same as a copy of the report of the Supreme Judicial Council (Annexure-G) and that there being no ingredients or finding as to the "guilty of gross misconduct" in the report of the Council, the impugned order of removal is ex-facie without "jurisdiction and lawful authority" and hence the writ-petition and the instant Rule. 

 7. The writ petitioner has submitted that under the provisions of Article—96(6) the Hon'ble President has been empowered to remove a judge from his office, if after making inquiry, the Supreme Judicial Council reports to the President that in its opinion (i) the Judge has ceased to be capable of properly performing the functions of his office; or (ii) the Judge has been guilty of gross misconduct. The writ petitioner taking us through the report of the Supreme Judicial Council (Annexure-G) to the writ petition) submits that the Supreme Judicial Council has clearly found (i) that the allegations against the writ petitioner were not proved beyond doubt; and that (ii) the allegation of payment of money to the writ petitioner has not been corroborated by the persons, who said to have went with Mrs. Kona to the residence of the writ petitioner and that (iii) none of the witnesses has said or claimed to have seen payment of money to the writ petitioner by Mrs. Kona; and that (iv) neither Pavel nor Mona, who said to have accompanied Mrs. Kona to the residence of writ petitioner as alleged, have been brought before the Supreme Judicial Council. The writ petitioner further submitted that the Hon'ble President has been given the authority to deal with the issue of removal of any Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh only under the provisions of Article—96(6) and that Article-96(2) of the Constitution provides that a Judge shall not be removed from office except in accordance with the following provisions of "this article" meaning thereby Article 96. The writ petitioner referring to Article-94(2) of the Constitution submitted that the word "Judge" appearing in Article-96 means and includes any Judge of the Appellate Division as well as of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and Article 96(4) provides that the function of the Supreme Judicial Council is to enquire as to the capacity or conduct of a Judge or of any other functionary, who is not removable from office except in like manner as a Judge, and also to prescribe a Code of Conduct to be observed by the Judges; and that Article 96(5) provides, amongst others, that the Hon'ble President may direct the Supreme Judicial Council to enquire into any allegation of "gross misconduct" on the part of a Judge and to report its finding to him, if he has reason to apprehend that such judge may be guilty of gross-misconduct and therefore the Hon'ble President require to have a preliminary enquiry to justify his reason to such apprehension but such preliminary opinion of the Hon'ble President is absent in his case and that the report reveals that the Supreme Judicial Council has gone beyond the authority given by Article 96(5) of the Constitution, in that the Supreme Judicial Council having found that the allegations against the writ petitioner have not been proved, which is its definite finding, as required under Article 96(5) of the Constitution, it's opinion that the writ petitioner "should not continue as Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh" is unwarranted and without jurisdiction, since provisions of Article 96(5) permit the Supreme Judicial Council only to give its finding on the reference made under Article 96(4) of the Constitution. 

 8. The Writ petitioner then submits that the Hon'ble President has acted without jurisdiction and authority in passing the impugned order of removal since that the provisions of Article 96(6) authorized the Hon'ble President to remove a Judge from office only on receipt of an opinion of the Supreme Judicial Council to the effect the Judge concern has been "guilty of gross misconduct" and that Article 96(5), amongst others, empowers the Hon'ble President to refer a matter to the Supreme Judicial Council for enquiry if he has reason to apprehend that a Judge may have been "guilty of gross misconduct" and which also reflects from Annexure-F to the writ petition, in as much as the Council did not found the writ petitioner "guilty" of any allegation and accordingly the opinion of the Council as reflected in the report did not mention anything about "gross-misconduct" and thus the impugned order of removal of the writ petitioner is the result of non-application of mind on the part of the Hon'ble President. The writ petitioner further submitted that the decision of the President in removing a Judge of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh is of grave nature and such order need be passed on proper scrutiny and on due consideration and examination of all available materials, particularly the inquiry report of the Supreme Judicial Council, and the findings of the Supreme Judicial Council required under Articles 96(5) ought to be given due weight. The writ petitioner summing up his submission asserted that in the absence, of finding of "guilty of gross misconduct" against the writ petitioner by the Supreme Judicial Council as mandated by Article 96(5) and (6) of the Constitution, the impugned order of removal of the writ petitioner by the Hon'ble President under Article 96(6) of the Constitution is without jurisdiction and without lawful authority and of no legal effect. 

 9. The learned Attorney General, after reading the Rule, as issued, the report of the Supreme Judicial Council (Annexure-G) and the provisions of the Article 96(6) of the Constitution with us, found it difficult to support the impugned order of removal. The learned Attorney General having found from the report (Annexure-G) that the Supreme Judicial Counsel has held that the allegations brought against the writ petitioner have not been proved beyond doubt and there being absence of any finding as to "guilty of gross-misconduct" against the writ petitioner, had no alternative but to concede that the impugned order as passed is not is accordance with the provisions of Article 96(6) of the Constitution and is without jurisdiction inasmuch since Article 96(6) gave the mandate to the Hon'ble President to remove the writ petitioner "only" if the Council could find the writ petitioner "guilty of gross-misconduct" in the instant case. 

 (b) may have been guilty of gross misconduct, the President may direct the Council to inquire into the matter and report its finding 

 (6) If, after making the inquiry, the Council reports to the Presidents that in its opinion the Judge has ceased to be capable of properly performing the functions of his office or has been guilty of gross misconduct, the President shall, by order remove the Judge from office. 

 From plain reading of the provisions of sub-articles of Article 96 we find that Article 96(2) provides that a Judge shall not be removed from office except in accordance with the provisions of this Article meaning there by Article 96, and that Article 96(6) provides that after an inquiry is made, the Supreme Judicial Council shall submit a report and if in the said report, containing its findings as required under Section 96(5), the Council makes an opinion to the effect that (i) the Judge has ceased to be capable of property performing the functions of his office; or (ii) the Judge has been found guilty of gross-misconduct; then and "only than" the Hon'ble President derives his authority under Article 96(6) to remove a Judge from office otherwise not, Article 96(4) prescribed the functions of Supreme Judicial Council, which amongst others, empowers it to enquire into the conduct of a Judge, if so required by the Hon'ble President and in such case the President may direct the Council to inquire into any allegation and submit report with finding and such allegation must relate to commission of any gross misconduct. In the instant case though, as it appears from the materials available on record that the allegation has been brought against the writ petitioner as to receipt of money from Mrs. Kona in connection with a bail matter but the Council has found that such allegation has not been proved. Thus the question of "guilty of gross misconduct" does not arise and in fact the Supreme Judicial Council did not give any opinion of the effect the writ petitioner has been found "guilty of any misconduct" not to speak of guilty of gross misconduct" as required to attract the provisions of Article 96(6) of the Constitution. 

 14. Article —96(5) has authorized the Council to give its finding as to whether the judge concern (i) has ceased to be capable of properly performing his functions of his office because of physical or mental incapacity, or (ii) is guilty of gross misconduct But in the report the Council, in spite of its finding that allegations have not been proved also, opined that the writ petitioner should not continue as Judge of the High- Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, which is, ex-facie, beyond the scope of Article-96(5) of the Constitution and therefore such portion of opinion contained in the report is without jurisdiction in as much as in the absence of proof of the alleged payment of money to the writ-petitioner by Mrs. Kona, the allegations against the writ petitioner are baseless. The mere statement of Mrs. Kona against the writ petitioner cannot be entertained as basis of an allegation, more so when such is made against any judicial official not to speak of any person holding a constitutional office.
